title: Planes Across the U.S. Stop Flying After Rare Nationwide Ground Stop
summary:
On Friday, planes across the United States stopped flying. The Federal Aviation Administration, the agency that keeps air travel safe, ordered a rare nationwide ground stop. It said the step was needed for "extraordinary circumstances" and "reasons of safety." Runways emptied, and hundreds of flights were affected.

A ground stop means planes stay on the ground instead of taking off. Air traffic controllers still guide the planes already in the sky to safe landings. The order covered the whole country at once, which almost never happens. It was only the third nationwide grounding in recent decades. The last one came in January 2023, when a pilot communications system failed.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters that officials did not believe the problem was tied to a specific attack. He said it appeared to be a telecommunication outage, a failure in the systems that let controllers and pilots talk to each other. He also said there was no reason for the public to be afraid.

What exactly went wrong is still unclear. Aviation correspondent Miles O'Brien said 22 regional centers manage planes flying at cruise altitude across the country. The centers are linked by simple landlines, old-fashioned phone lines. Some experts think the link between the centers failed. Others wonder whether hacking played a part, or whether the trouble comes from the system's age. Parts of it still use floppy disks, paper strips, and radar equipment dating back to the 1940s.

One flight tracker showed planes across the country standing still, marked in yellow. Travel is at an all-time high, and O'Brien said the system is bursting at the seams. He praised the air traffic controllers who keep it working every day. Everyone was safe, he said, though many travelers were extremely inconvenienced.
why_it_matters: Air travel is how millions of people move around the country, so when the whole system stops, families, trips, and plans everywhere are affected. The story also shows why the old systems that keep planes safe need to be kept up to date.

background_read: The Federal Aviation Administration, or FAA, is the part of the U.S. government that keeps flying safe.
Air traffic controllers guide planes through the sky and tell pilots when to take off and land, working from centers spread across the country.
A ground stop is an order that keeps planes on the ground, used when something makes flying unsafe.
The system that guides planes is very old in places, and it has many backup layers so that one failure does not stop everything.
